title: What can you say about lion's mane in your ads and on your site?
summary: The library supports 1 wording for lion's mane; the strongest is "A source of fungal polysaccharides and antioxidants" (limited, up to 2.8 g dried fruiting body or mycelium a day). Avoid wording that names or implies a disease, a drug or a treatment, such as "Improves memory in dementia or Alzheimer's disease".

supported_wordings.wording: A source of fungal polysaccharides and antioxidants.
supported_wordings.why: Health Canada sets a maximum dose only; no other listed source covers it.
supported_wordings.daily_dose: up to 2.8 g dried fruiting body or mycelium a day
supported_wordings.dose_details: Up to 2.8 g a day, dry or powdered, per Health Canada; no minimum is set.
supported_wordings.form: Dried or powdered fruiting body or mycelium

wordings_to_avoid.wording: Improves memory in dementia or Alzheimer's disease

wordings_to_avoid.why: Implies repair of a damaged body system; no listed source supports it.

evidence_strengths.strong: At least two listed sources support it independently at a comparable dose and form, and none disagrees.
evidence_strengths.moderate: One listed source supports it as an evidence-based use at that dose, and no listed source disagrees.
evidence_strengths.limited: The only support is traditional use, the sources disagree, or the source itself calls the evidence weak.

reasons_to_avoid.drug: names a drug or presents the product as one
reasons_to_avoid.treatment: promises to treat, cure or prevent a condition

disclaimer: Not legal advice. This guide shows the wording that published evidence supports at a daily dose, from the sources linked below; it is not a ruling on any claim. Your own product, its form and dose, and your own evidence still need to match the wording you use.
